decks.title: Derivatives - Part 1: Rate of change, tangents and first principles
goals: Find average and instantaneous velocity from a distance-time function
Read the derivative as the slope of a tangent and write the tangent at a point
Differentiate powers, square roots, reciprocals, sine and cosine from the definition
Find the derivative at a point from the limit definition

slides.heading: Derivatives, Part 1
slides.body_md: From average speed to the slope of a curve at a single point.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: average and instantaneous velocity, the slope of a tangent, the definition of the derivative as a limit, derivatives of powers, square roots and reciprocals from the definition, and then sine and cosine.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on derivatives. In this first part we start with a moving body and ask how fast it is going at one instant. That leads to the slope of a tangent and to the definition of the derivative as a limit. We then differentiate powers, roots, reciprocals, sine and cosine directly from that definition. Every result was checked numerically.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Use the derivative as the **slope of a tangent**
Evaluate a **derivative at a point** from a limit

rows: Find an average and an instantaneous velocity
Find the slope and equation of a tangent

visual.alt: Table of goals for Part 1: velocity from a distance-time function, the tangent equation, the definition of the derivative, derivatives of powers, roots and reciprocals from the definition, and derivatives of sine and cosine.
visual.caption: What Part 1 covers.

slides.narration: By the end of this part you will find an average and an instantaneous velocity from a distance function. You will use the derivative as the slope of a tangent, and write the tangent at a point. You will differentiate from the definition, including sine and cosine, and find a derivative at a point from a limit. The table shows the key result for each skill.

slides.heading: Average velocity
slides.body_md: A trolley has travelled $s = t^2 + 3t$ metres after $t$ seconds. Over the time from $t$ to $t + h$ its **average velocity** is the change in distance divided by the time taken.

visual.alt: Table for a trolley with distance s equal to t squared plus 3 t metres: over the interval from 2 seconds to 2 plus h seconds the average velocity is 8, 7.5, 7.1 and 7.01 metres per second for h equal to 1, 0.5, 0.1 and 0.01, which is 7 plus h and approaches 7.
visual.caption: Average velocity on $[2, 2 + h]$ is $7 + h$.

slides.narration: Average velocity is the distance covered divided by the time taken. For a trolley whose distance is t squared plus three t metres, the average velocity from two seconds to two plus h seconds works out to seven plus h. As h gets smaller, the average velocity gets closer to seven. The table shows eight, seven point five, seven point one and seven point zero one.

slides.heading: Instantaneous velocity
slides.body_md: The velocity at the single instant $t$ is the number that the average velocities approach as $h$ shrinks to $0$. On the distance-time graph, the average velocity is the slope of a **secant** and the instantaneous velocity is the slope of the **tangent**.

visual.alt: Distance-time graph of s equal to t squared plus 3 t. The secant through P at t equal to 2 and Q at t equal to 3 has slope 8, the average velocity; the tangent at P has slope 7, the instantaneous velocity.
visual.caption: Secant slope $8$ (average), tangent slope $7$ (instantaneous).

slides.narration: The instantaneous velocity is the limit of the average velocities as h tends to zero. On the graph, the secant through the points P and Q has slope eight, the average velocity. The tangent at P has slope seven, the instantaneous velocity at two seconds. The limit of the secant slopes is the tangent slope. This limit is called the derivative of the distance with respect to time.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a cart
slides.body_md: A cart has $s = 2t^2 + 5t$ metres at $t$ seconds. Find the average velocity from $t = 1$ to $t = 3$ and the velocity at $t = 1$.

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: for s equal to 2 t squared plus 5 t, the average velocity from t equal to 1 to t equal to 3 is 26 divided by 2, which is 13 metres per second, and the quotient from t equal to 1 is 9 plus 2 h, which tends to 9 metres per second.
visual.caption: Average and instantaneous velocity of one cart.

slides.narration: First the average velocity. The distance at one second is seven metres and at three seconds is thirty three metres, so the average velocity is twenty six divided by two, which is thirteen metres per second. For the velocity at one second, the quotient simplifies to nine plus two h. Letting h tend to zero gives nine metres per second.

slides.heading: Quick check: a velocity
slides.body_md: Find the instantaneous velocity of a trolley with a simple distance function at a given time.
slides.narration: Find the derivative of the distance function, then substitute the time.

slides.heading: Secants approaching the tangent
slides.body_md: Fix a point $P$ on a curve and let $Q$ approach $P$. The slopes of the secants $PQ$ approach a limit, which is the slope of the **tangent** at $P$.

visual.alt: Plot of y equal to x squared minus 4 x plus 5 with P at 3, 2. The secant to Q1 at 5, 10 has slope 4, the secant to Q2 at 4, 5 has slope 3, and the tangent at P has slope 2: the secant slopes decrease to the tangent slope as Q approaches P.
visual.caption: Secant slopes $4$, $3$, ... approach the tangent slope $2$.

slides.narration: Take the point P at three comma two on a curve. The secant to Q one has slope four, and the secant to Q two has slope three. As Q moves closer to P along the curve, the secant slopes keep decreasing towards two. That limit, two, is the slope of the tangent at P, and it is the derivative at that point.

slides.heading: Tangent at a point
slides.body_md: The slope of the tangent at $x = a$ is $f'(a)$, so the tangent through $(a, f(a))$ is given by the point-slope form.

visual.alt: Table that finds the tangent to y equal to x squared minus 4 x plus 5 at x equal to 3: f of 3 is 2, the difference quotient is 2 plus h which tends to 2, so the tangent is y minus 2 equals 2 times x minus 3, which is y equal to 2 x minus 4.
visual.caption: Tangent: $y - f(a) = f'(a)(x - a)$.

slides.narration: To write a tangent, find the point and the slope. The point is a comma f of a. The slope is f dash of a, the derivative at that point. Then use the point slope form, y minus f of a equals f dash of a times x minus a. The table does this for a curve at x equal to three, and finds a tangent with slope two.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: tangent from the definition
slides.body_md: Find the slope of the tangent to $y = 3x^2 - x$ at $x = 2$, and the equation of the tangent.

visual.alt: Plot of y equal to 3 x squared minus x and its tangent y equal to 11 x minus 12 at the point 2, 10, where both pass.
visual.caption: Slope $11$ at $x = 2$.

slides.narration: The point of contact is two comma ten. The quotient for f of two plus h minus f of two, over h, simplifies to eleven plus three h, which tends to eleven. So the slope of the tangent is eleven. The tangent is y minus ten equals eleven times x minus two, which is y equals eleven x minus twelve. The picture shows it touching the curve at that point.

slides.heading: Quick check: average velocity
slides.body_md: Find an average velocity over an interval from the distances at its two ends.
slides.narration: Divide the change in distance by the change in time.

slides.heading: The definition of the derivative
slides.body_md: The **derivative** of $f$ at $x$ is the limit of the difference quotient. Work in four steps: write $f(x + h)$, form the quotient, simplify and cancel $h$, then let $h \to 0$.

nodes.label: Write f of x plus h

visual.alt: Flow chart of differentiation from first principles: write f of x plus h, form the difference quotient, simplify and cancel the factor h, then let h tend to zero.
visual.caption: Four steps of the definition.

slides.narration: The derivative of f at x is the limit of f of x plus h minus f of x, all over h, as h tends to zero. Work in four steps. Write f of x plus h. Form the difference quotient. Simplify it and cancel the factor h. Only then let h tend to zero. Taking the limit before cancelling always gives zero over zero.

slides.heading: Powers, roots and reciprocals
slides.body_md: For $x^n$ with a positive integer $n$ the binomial theorem gives $\dfrac{(x + h)^n - x^n}{h} = nx^{n - 1} + \dots$ with every other term containing $h$. A square root is rationalised, and a reciprocal is put over a common denominator.

visual.alt: Table of first-principles results: x squared has quotient 2 x plus h and derivative 2 x; x cubed has quotient 3 x squared plus 3 x h plus h squared and derivative 3 x squared; the square root of x has derivative 1 over 2 root x; 1 over x has derivative minus 1 over x squared.
visual.caption: Each quotient equals $\dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$ exactly.

slides.narration: For x to the n, expand x plus h to the n with the binomial theorem. After subtracting x to the n and dividing by h, the first term is n x to the n minus one and every other term still has h in it. For the square root, multiply by the conjugate. For a reciprocal, use a common denominator. The table lists four results.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a reciprocal
slides.body_md: Differentiate $\dfrac{1}{x + 3}$ from first principles, for $x \ne -3$.

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table: the difference quotient of 1 over x plus 3 simplifies to minus 1 over x plus h plus 3 times x plus 3, and as h tends to zero the derivative is minus 1 over x plus 3 all squared.
visual.caption: Combine the fractions, then cancel $h$.

slides.narration: Write the quotient with a common denominator. The numerator becomes x plus three minus x plus h plus three, which is minus h. The factor h cancels, leaving minus one over x plus h plus three, times x plus three. Now let h tend to zero. The derivative is minus one over x plus three all squared.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a square root
slides.body_md: Differentiate $\sqrt{x}$ from first principles for $x > 0$, and find the value at $x = 9$.
bullets: Multiply by the conjugate: quotient $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}}$

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table: rationalising the difference quotient of the square root of x gives 1 over the square root of x plus h plus the square root of x, so the derivative is 1 over 2 root x, which is 1 over 6 at x equal to 9.
visual.caption: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.

slides.narration: The quotient is root of x plus h minus root of x, over h. Multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate, root of x plus h plus root of x. The numerator becomes h, which cancels. We are left with one over root of x plus h plus root of x. As h tends to zero this is one over two root x. At x equal to nine it is one sixth.

slides.heading: Sine and cosine
slides.body_md: Two standard limits are needed, with angles in radians. Sine and cosine are differentiated by splitting the quotient into these.

visual.alt: Table of values: for h equal to 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 and 0.0001 radians, sine h over h is 0.998334, 0.999983, 1.000000 and 1.000000 and cosine h minus 1 over h is minus 0.049958, minus 0.005, minus 0.0005 and minus 0.00005, so the limits are 1 and 0.
visual.caption: $\dfrac{\sin h}{h} \to 1$ and $\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h} \to 0$.

slides.narration: For sine and cosine we need two standard limits. Sine h over h tends to one, and cosine h minus one over h tends to zero. The table shows values for h equal to point one, point zero one and smaller. Expand sine of x plus h, split the quotient, and use these limits. The result is that sine has derivative cosine, and cosine has derivative minus sine.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: sine of 2x
slides.body_md: Differentiate $\sin 2x$ from first principles.

rows: $\sin C - \sin D = 2\cos\dfrac{C + D}{2}\sin\dfrac{C - D}{2} \Rightarrow 2\cos(2x + h)\sin h$

visual.alt: Worked example 5 table: the difference quotient of sine 2 x equals 2 cosine of 2 x plus h times sine h over h, which tends to 2 cosine 2 x.
visual.caption: Uses $\dfrac{\sin h}{h} \to 1$.

slides.narration: Write sine of two x plus two h minus sine of two x as a product, using the formula for the difference of two sines. It becomes two cosine of two x plus h, times sine h. Dividing by h leaves two cosine of two x plus h, times sine h over h. As h tends to zero this tends to two cosine two x. Notice the factor two from the argument.

slides.heading: Quick check: a reciprocal at a point
slides.body_md: Decide whether a stated derivative of a reciprocal at a point is correct.
slides.narration: Use the quotient from the definition and let h tend to zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a derivative at a point
slides.body_md: Find $f'(2)$ for $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ using $f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a}\dfrac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$.

visual.alt: Worked example 6 table: for f of x equal to 1 over x, the quotient f of x minus f of 2 over x minus 2 simplifies to minus 1 over 2 x, so f dash of 2 is minus one quarter.
visual.caption: The derivative at a point as a limit in $x$.

slides.narration: There is a second form of the definition. The derivative at a is the limit, as x tends to a, of f of x minus f of a, over x minus a. For one over x at two, the numerator is two minus x over two x. Since two minus x is minus x minus two, the factor x minus two cancels, leaving minus one over two x. At x equal to two the derivative is minus one quarter.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Average velocity $\dfrac{s(t + h) - s(t)}{h}$; velocity is its limit, the derivative
The derivative is the **slope of the tangent**; tangent $y - f(a) = f'(a)(x - a)$
Simplify the difference quotient before letting $h \to 0$

visual.alt: Summary table for Part 1: average velocity, the definition of the derivative, the tangent equation, the derivatives of powers, the square root and the reciprocal, and of sine and cosine.
visual.caption: Part 1 in five lines.

slides.narration: To sum up. Average velocity is the change in distance over the time taken, and the instantaneous velocity is its limit, which is the derivative. The derivative is also the slope of the tangent, so the tangent at a point follows from the point slope form. In first principles, simplify the quotient first, then let h tend to zero. And remember the results for powers, the square root, sine and cosine.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Simplify the quotient **before** taking the limit
Use the binomial theorem for $(x + h)^n$
Rationalise square roots; use a common denominator for reciprocals
Angles are in radians whenever sine or cosine is differentiated

rows: Write the quotient, then simplify, then take the limit
The limit is taken only after $h$ has been cancelled
Expand $(x + h)^n$ with the binomial theorem
Only the first two terms matter after dividing by $h$
Quote $\dfrac{\sin h}{h} \to 1$ for sine and cosine

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1: simplify before taking the limit, expand with the binomial theorem, rationalise square roots, and quote the standard limit with angles in radians.
visual.caption: How to set out first principles.

slides.narration: In the examination, simplify the difference quotient before taking the limit, and show the cancelled factor h. Use the binomial theorem for powers, rationalise square roots, and use a common denominator for reciprocals. When you differentiate sine or cosine, quote the standard limit and remember that angles are in radians. State the final derivative clearly.

decks.title: Derivatives - Part 2: Rules and standard derivatives
goals: Differentiate sums, differences and constant multiples term by term
Use the product rule and the quotient rule, with checks
Differentiate the six trigonometric functions and combinations
Use the derivative at a point for slopes, tangents and rates of change

slides.heading: Derivatives, Part 2
slides.body_md: Rules that replace the limit: sums, products, quotients and trigonometric functions.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the standard derivatives, sums, differences and constant multiples, the product rule, the quotient rule, and trigonometric functions with applications to slopes and rates.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to the second part on derivatives. Doing a limit every time is slow, so we now use rules. We start with the standard derivatives and with sums and constant multiples. Then come the product rule and the quotient rule, the derivatives of tangent, secant, cosecant and cotangent, and finally slopes and rates of change. Each result was checked numerically.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Use a **derivative at a point** for slope and rate

rows: Use a derivative at a point
tangent slope, horizontal tangent, rate of change

visual.alt: Table of goals for Part 2: sums and constant multiples, the product rule, the quotient rule, derivatives of the six trigonometric functions, and slopes and rates from a derivative at a point.
visual.caption: What Part 2 covers.

slides.narration: In this part you will differentiate sums and constant multiples term by term. You will apply the product rule and the quotient rule. You will differentiate the six trigonometric functions. And you will use a derivative at a point to find a slope, a tangent or a rate of change. The table lists the key result for each skill.

slides.heading: Standard derivatives
slides.body_md: These results are used every time. The angle in each trigonometric function is in radians, and a function is differentiated only where it is defined.

visual.alt: Table of standard derivatives: a constant has derivative 0, x to the n has n x to the n minus 1, sine gives cosine, cosine gives minus sine, tangent gives secant squared, secant gives secant tangent, cosecant gives minus cosecant cotangent, and cotangent gives minus cosecant squared.
visual.caption: The eight standard results (angles in radians).

slides.narration: Here are the standard derivatives. A constant has derivative zero. X to the n has derivative n x to the n minus one. Sine gives cosine, and cosine gives minus sine. Tangent gives secant squared. Secant gives secant tangent. Cosecant gives minus cosecant cotangent, and cotangent gives minus cosecant squared. The three functions that begin with co all carry a minus sign.

slides.heading: Sums, differences and constant multiples
slides.body_md: A constant factor stays outside, and a sum or difference is differentiated term by term.

visual.alt: Table of the linearity rules: a constant multiple, a sum, a difference, and a whole expression differentiated term by term, each with a worked example.
visual.caption: Differentiate term by term; a constant factor stays.

slides.narration: A constant factor stays in front when we differentiate. A sum or a difference is differentiated term by term. So to differentiate four x cubed minus five sine x plus seven, we get twelve x squared minus five cosine x, and the constant seven disappears. The table gives an example of each rule, all checked numerically.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a polynomial at a point
slides.body_md: Find $f'(x)$ and $f'(2)$ for $f(x) = x^4 - 6x^2 + 3x - 7$.

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: the derivative of x to the fourth minus 6 x squared plus 3 x minus 7 is 4 x cubed minus 12 x plus 3, whose value at x equal to 2 is 32 minus 24 plus 3, which is 11.
visual.caption: Power rule on each term, then substitute.

slides.narration: Differentiate each term. X to the fourth gives four x cubed. Minus six x squared gives minus twelve x. Three x gives three, and the constant minus seven gives zero. So f dash of x is four x cubed minus twelve x plus three. At x equal to two this is thirty two minus twenty four plus three, which is eleven.

slides.heading: Quick check: a derivative at a point
slides.body_md: Differentiate a quadratic and evaluate the derivative at a given value of $x$.
slides.narration: Differentiate each term, then substitute.

slides.heading: The product rule
slides.body_md: The derivative of a product is **not** the product of the derivatives.

visual.alt: Table for the product rule applied to x squared times x cubed plus 1: the rule and direct expansion both give 5 x to the fourth plus 2 x, while multiplying the two derivatives gives 6 x cubed, which is wrong.
visual.caption: $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$, not $u'v'$.

slides.narration: The derivative of a product is the derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times the derivative of the second. It is not the product of the two derivatives. In the table, x squared times x cubed plus one is differentiated by the rule and also by expanding first. Both give five x to the fourth plus two x. Multiplying the derivatives gives six x cubed, which is wrong.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a polynomial product
slides.body_md: Differentiate $(x^2 + 3)(2x - 5)$ by the product rule and check by expanding.
bullets: $= 6x^2 - 10x + 6$; expanding gives $2x^3 - 5x^2 + 6x - 15$, with the same derivative

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table: the product x squared plus 3 times 2 x minus 5 has derivative 2 x times 2 x minus 5 plus 2 times x squared plus 3, which simplifies to 6 x squared minus 10 x plus 6; expanding first gives the same.
visual.caption: Two routes, one answer.

slides.narration: Let u be x squared plus three and v be two x minus five. Then u dash is two x and v dash is two. The rule gives two x times two x minus five, plus two times x squared plus three. This simplifies to six x squared minus ten x plus six. As a check, expand the product first to get two x cubed minus five x squared plus six x minus fifteen, and differentiate. The answers agree.

slides.heading: The quotient rule
slides.body_md: For $v \ne 0$, the derivative of a quotient has the **denominator times the derivative of the top, minus the top times the derivative of the denominator**, over the denominator squared.

visual.alt: Table for the quotient rule applied to x squared over x plus 2: the numerator is 2 x times x plus 2 minus x squared, which is x squared plus 4 x, so the derivative is x squared plus 4 x over x plus 2 all squared.
visual.caption: Bottom times derivative of top, minus top times derivative of bottom, over bottom squared.

slides.narration: The quotient rule says: the derivative of u over v is u dash v minus u v dash, all over v squared. The order in the numerator matters, because of the minus sign. In the table, u is x squared and v is x plus two. The numerator is two x times x plus two, minus x squared, which is x squared plus four x. The denominator is x plus two all squared.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a quotient
slides.body_md: Differentiate $\dfrac{x^2 - 2}{x + 1}$ for $x \ne -1$ and check at $x = 1$.

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table: the quotient x squared minus 2 over x plus 1 has numerator 2 x times x plus 1 minus x squared minus 2, which is x squared plus 2 x plus 2, so the derivative is x squared plus 2 x plus 2 over x plus 1 all squared, and at x equal to 1 it is five quarters.
visual.caption: Always state where $v \ne 0$.

slides.narration: Let u be x squared minus two and v be x plus one. Then u dash is two x and v dash is one. The numerator is two x times x plus one, minus x squared minus two. That is x squared plus two x plus two. The derivative is that over x plus one all squared. At x equal to one it is five over four. State that x is not minus one.

slides.heading: Quick check: a product
slides.body_md: Decide whether the derivative of a product equals the product of the derivatives.
slides.narration: Differentiate the product after simplifying it, and compare.

slides.heading: Tangent, secant, cosecant and cotangent
slides.body_md: Write each function in terms of sine and cosine and use the quotient rule. Secant, cosecant and cotangent follow the same pattern, so check each sign.

rows: $\dfrac{\cos x \cdot \cos x - \sin x(-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} = \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x}$
$\dfrac{-\sin x \cdot \sin x - \cos x\cos x}{\sin^2 x} = -\dfrac{1}{\sin^2 x}$

visual.alt: Table that derives the derivatives of tangent, secant, cosecant and cotangent by the quotient rule from sine and cosine, giving secant squared, secant tangent, minus cosecant cotangent and minus cosecant squared.
visual.caption: The quotient rule explains the four new results.

slides.narration: The new standard results come from the quotient rule. Write tangent as sine over cosine. The numerator is cosine times cosine plus sine times sine, which is one, so the derivative is one over cosine squared, secant squared. In the same way secant gives secant tangent, cosecant gives minus cosecant cotangent, and cotangent gives minus cosecant squared. The table shows all four.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a product with a trigonometric factor
slides.body_md: Differentiate $x\tan x - 2\operatorname{cosec} x$ where it is defined.
bullets: Result $\tan x + x\sec^2 x + 2\operatorname{cosec} x\cot x$

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table: the function x tangent x minus 2 cosecant x has derivative tangent x plus x secant squared x plus 2 cosecant x cotangent x, using the product rule on the first term and a standard result on the second.
visual.caption: Product rule for one term, standard result for the other.

slides.narration: Split the function into two terms. For x tangent x, use the product rule. One times tangent x, plus x times secant squared x. For two cosecant x, use the standard result, which gives minus two cosecant x cotangent x. Because the second term is subtracted, its derivative is added. The result is tangent x plus x secant squared x plus two cosecant x cotangent x.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: secant times tangent
slides.body_md: Differentiate $\sec x\tan x$ where it is defined.
bullets: $u = \sec x$, $v = \tan x$: $\sec x\tan x \cdot \tan x + \sec x \cdot \sec^2 x$
$= \sec x\tan^2 x + \sec^3 x = \sec x\left(\tan^2 x + \sec^2 x\right)$

rows: $u = \sec x, \; v = \tan x \Rightarrow u' = \sec x\tan x, \; v' = \sec^2 x$

visual.alt: Worked example 5 table: the product secant x times tangent x has derivative secant x tangent squared x plus secant cubed x, which factorises as secant x times tangent squared x plus secant squared x.
visual.caption: Two standard results inside the product rule.

slides.narration: Let u be secant x and v be tangent x. Then u dash is secant x tangent x and v dash is secant squared x. The product rule gives secant x tangent squared x, plus secant cubed x. We may factorise this as secant x times tangent squared x plus secant squared x. Either form is accepted as the answer.

slides.heading: Linear arguments
slides.body_md: For a linear argument the factor of $x$ comes out: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(ax + b) = a\cos(ax + b)$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos(ax + b) = -a\sin(ax + b)$. A power such as $(3x + 2)^2$ is expanded first.

rows: the factor $3$ from the linear argument
the factor $2$ appears, and the sign changes

visual.alt: Table for linear arguments: sine 3 x has derivative 3 cosine 3 x, cosine of 2 x minus 1 has derivative minus 2 sine of 2 x minus 1, and 3 x plus 2 all squared is expanded to 9 x squared plus 12 x plus 4 with derivative 18 x plus 12.
visual.caption: For $\sin(ax + b)$ the derivative is $a\cos(ax + b)$.

slides.narration: When the angle is a linear expression such as three x, the factor of x comes out in front. Sine of three x has derivative three cosine of three x. Cosine of two x minus one has derivative minus two sine of two x minus one. For a power such as three x plus two all squared, expand it first and then differentiate. That gives eighteen x plus twelve.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a rate of change
slides.body_md: An oven's temperature is $T = 3t^2 - 18t + 200$ degrees Celsius after $t$ minutes, for $0 \le t \le 6$. Find the rate of change at $t = 1$ and when it is zero.

rows: $T = 3t^2 - 18t + 200, \quad 0 \le t \le 6$, with $T$ in degrees Celsius and $t$ in minutes
$6 - 18 = -12$: falling at 12 degrees Celsius per minute

visual.alt: Worked example 6 table: an oven temperature of 3 t squared minus 18 t plus 200 degrees Celsius has rate of change 6 t minus 18, which is minus 12 at t equal to 1 and zero at t equal to 3, when the temperature is 173 degrees.
visual.caption: The derivative is the rate of change with time.

slides.narration: The rate of change of temperature with time is the derivative. It is six t minus eighteen. At one minute it is minus twelve, so the oven is cooling by twelve degrees every minute. The rate is zero when six t minus eighteen is zero, that is at three minutes. The temperature at that moment is one hundred and seventy three degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: a tangent slope
slides.body_md: Find the gradient of a tangent to a quartic graph at a given point.
slides.narration: The slope of the tangent is the derivative at that point.

slides.heading: Horizontal tangents
slides.body_md: The tangent is parallel to the $x$-axis where the slope is zero, so solve $f'(x) = 0$ and then find the $y$-coordinates from $f$.

visual.alt: Plot of y equal to x cubed minus 3 x with horizontal tangents y equal to 2 at x equal to minus 1 and y equal to minus 2 at x equal to 1, the two points where the derivative 3 x squared minus 3 is zero.
visual.caption: Horizontal tangent where $f'(x) = 0$.

slides.narration: A tangent is parallel to the x axis where its slope is zero. So solve f dash of x equals zero, then find the heights from the original function. notes.title: Derivatives - chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Average and instantaneous rate of change
sections.body_md:
For a distance-time function $s(t)$, the **average velocity** over $[t, t + h]$ is $\dfrac{s(t + h) - s(t)}{h}$. The **instantaneous velocity** is the limit of this as $h \to 0$, written $s'(t)$ or $\dfrac{ds}{dt}$.

More generally the derivative is the rate of change of one quantity with respect to another, for example the rate at which the volume of a tank or the temperature of an oven changes with time. Its sign shows increase or decrease.

key_terms.definition_md: Change in distance divided by the time taken, over a whole interval.
The limit of the average velocities as the interval shrinks to zero; the derivative of distance with respect to time.

visual.alt: Table for a trolley with distance s equal to t squared plus 3 t metres: over the interval from 2 seconds to 2 plus h seconds the average velocity is 8, 7.5, 7.1 and 7.01 metres per second for h equal to 1, 0.5, 0.1 and 0.01, which is 7 plus h and approaches 7.
visual.caption: Average velocity on $[2, 2 + h]$ is $7 + h$.

visuals.alt: Distance-time graph of s equal to t squared plus 3 t. The secant through P at t equal to 2 and Q at t equal to 3 has slope 8, the average velocity; the tangent at P has slope 7, the instantaneous velocity.
visuals.caption: Secant slope $8$ (average), tangent slope $7$ (instantaneous).

visuals.alt: Worked example 1 table: for s equal to 2 t squared plus 5 t, the average velocity from t equal to 1 to t equal to 3 is 26 divided by 2, which is 13 metres per second, and the quotient from t equal to 1 is 9 plus 2 h, which tends to 9 metres per second.
visuals.caption: Average and instantaneous velocity of one cart.

sections.heading: 2. The slope of a tangent
sections.body_md:
The slope of the secant through $P(a, f(a))$ and a nearby point $Q$ tends to a limit as $Q \to P$; this limit is the slope of the **tangent** at $P$ and equals $f'(a)$.

The tangent at $x = a$ is $y - f(a) = f'(a)(x - a)$. To find a point where the tangent has a given slope, solve $f'(x) = m$; where $f'(x) = 0$ the tangent is parallel to the $x$-axis.

key_terms.definition_md: A line through two points of a curve; its slope is an average rate of change.
The limiting position of the secants; its slope is the derivative at the point.

visual.alt: Plot of y equal to x squared minus 4 x plus 5 with P at 3, 2. The secant to Q1 at 5, 10 has slope 4, the secant to Q2 at 4, 5 has slope 3, and the tangent at P has slope 2: the secant slopes decrease to the tangent slope as Q approaches P.
visual.caption: Secant slopes $4$, $3$, ... approach the tangent slope $2$.

visuals.alt: Table that finds the tangent to y equal to x squared minus 4 x plus 5 at x equal to 3: f of 3 is 2, the difference quotient is 2 plus h which tends to 2, so the tangent is y minus 2 equals 2 times x minus 3, which is y equal to 2 x minus 4.
visuals.caption: Tangent: $y - f(a) = f'(a)(x - a)$.

visuals.alt: Plot of y equal to 3 x squared minus x and its tangent y equal to 11 x minus 12 at the point 2, 10, where both pass.
visuals.caption: Slope $11$ at $x = 2$.

sections.heading: 3. Differentiation from first principles
sections.body_md:
The **derivative** is $f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$. Simplify the quotient and cancel $h$ before the limit. For $x^n$ expand $(x + h)^n$ by the binomial theorem; rationalise for $\sqrt{x}$; use a common denominator for $\dfrac{1}{x + a}$.

The derivative at a single point can also be written $f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a}\dfrac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The expression $\dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$ whose limit is the derivative.
Finding a derivative directly from the limit definition.

nodes.label: Write f of x plus h

visual.alt: Flow chart of differentiation from first principles: write f of x plus h, form the difference quotient, simplify and cancel the factor h, then let h tend to zero.
visual.caption: Four steps of the definition.

visuals.alt: Table of first-principles results: x squared has quotient 2 x plus h and derivative 2 x; x cubed has quotient 3 x squared plus 3 x h plus h squared and derivative 3 x squared; the square root of x has derivative 1 over 2 root x; 1 over x has derivative minus 1 over x squared.
visuals.caption: Each quotient equals $\dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$ exactly.

visuals.alt: Worked example 3 table: the difference quotient of 1 over x plus 3 simplifies to minus 1 over x plus h plus 3 times x plus 3, and as h tends to zero the derivative is minus 1 over x plus 3 all squared.
visuals.caption: Combine the fractions, then cancel $h$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 4 table: rationalising the difference quotient of the square root of x gives 1 over the square root of x plus h plus the square root of x, so the derivative is 1 over 2 root x, which is 1 over 6 at x equal to 9.
visuals.caption: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.

visuals.alt: Worked example 6 table: for f of x equal to 1 over x, the quotient f of x minus f of 2 over x minus 2 simplifies to minus 1 over 2 x, so f dash of 2 is minus one quarter.
visuals.caption: The derivative at a point as a limit in $x$.

sections.heading: 4. Sine and cosine from first principles
sections.body_md:
With angles in radians, $\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\sin h}{h} = 1$ and $\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h} = 0$. Expanding $\sin(x + h)$ and splitting the quotient gives $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \cos x$; the same for cosine gives $-\sin x$.

For a linear argument the factor of $x$ appears: from the definition $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin 2x) = 2\cos 2x$, using $\sin C - \sin D = 2\cos\dfrac{C + D}{2}\sin\dfrac{C - D}{2}$.

visual.alt: Table of values: for h equal to 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 and 0.0001 radians, sine h over h is 0.998334, 0.999983, 1.000000 and 1.000000 and cosine h minus 1 over h is minus 0.049958, minus 0.005, minus 0.0005 and minus 0.00005, so the limits are 1 and 0.
visual.caption: $\dfrac{\sin h}{h} \to 1$ and $\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h} \to 0$.

rows: $\sin C - \sin D = 2\cos\dfrac{C + D}{2}\sin\dfrac{C - D}{2} \Rightarrow 2\cos(2x + h)\sin h$

visuals.alt: Worked example 5 table: the difference quotient of sine 2 x equals 2 cosine of 2 x plus h times sine h over h, which tends to 2 cosine 2 x.
visuals.caption: Uses $\dfrac{\sin h}{h} \to 1$.

sections.heading: 5. Standard derivatives, sums and constant multiples
sections.body_md:
The standard results are $(c)' = 0$, $(x^n)' = nx^{n - 1}$, $(\sin x)' = \cos x$, $(\cos x)' = -\sin x$, $(\tan x)' = \sec^2 x$, $(\sec x)' = \sec x\tan x$, $(\cot x)' = -\operatorname{cosec}^2 x$ and $(\operatorname{cosec} x)' = -\operatorname{cosec} x\cot x$.

A constant factor stays and a sum or difference is differentiated term by term. Rewrite $\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ and $\sqrt{x}$ as powers first. A derivative at a point is found by substituting after differentiating.

visual.alt: Table of standard derivatives: a constant has derivative 0, x to the n has n x to the n minus 1, sine gives cosine, cosine gives minus sine, tangent gives secant squared, secant gives secant tangent, cosecant gives minus cosecant cotangent, and cotangent gives minus cosecant squared.
visual.caption: The eight standard results (angles in radians).

visuals.alt: Table of the linearity rules: a constant multiple, a sum, a difference, and a whole expression differentiated term by term, each with a worked example.
visuals.caption: Differentiate term by term; a constant factor stays.

visuals.alt: Worked example 1 table: the derivative of x to the fourth minus 6 x squared plus 3 x minus 7 is 4 x cubed minus 12 x plus 3, whose value at x equal to 2 is 32 minus 24 plus 3, which is 11.
visuals.caption: Power rule on each term, then substitute.

sections.heading: 6. The product rule and the quotient rule
sections.body_md:
**Product rule:** $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$, not $u'v'$. **Quotient rule:** $\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)' = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$ with $v \ne 0$; the order of the terms in the numerator matters.

Name $u$, $v$, $u'$ and $v'$ first. For polynomials a product can also be expanded first, which gives a check. A numerical check at one value of $x$ catches sign slips.

key_terms.definition_md: The derivative of a product is the first times the derivative of the second plus the second times the derivative of the first.
The derivative of a quotient is the bottom times the derivative of the top, minus the top times the derivative of the bottom, over the bottom squared.

visual.alt: Table for the product rule applied to x squared times x cubed plus 1: the rule and direct expansion both give 5 x to the fourth plus 2 x, while multiplying the two derivatives gives 6 x cubed, which is wrong.
visual.caption: $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$, not $u'v'$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 2 table: the product x squared plus 3 times 2 x minus 5 has derivative 2 x times 2 x minus 5 plus 2 times x squared plus 3, which simplifies to 6 x squared minus 10 x plus 6; expanding first gives the same.
visuals.caption: Two routes, one answer.

visuals.alt: Table for the quotient rule applied to x squared over x plus 2: the numerator is 2 x times x plus 2 minus x squared, which is x squared plus 4 x, so the derivative is x squared plus 4 x over x plus 2 all squared.
visuals.caption: Bottom times derivative of top, minus top times derivative of bottom, over bottom squared.

visuals.alt: Worked example 3 table: the quotient x squared minus 2 over x plus 1 has numerator 2 x times x plus 1 minus x squared minus 2, which is x squared plus 2 x plus 2, so the derivative is x squared plus 2 x plus 2 over x plus 1 all squared, and at x equal to 1 it is five quarters.
visuals.caption: Always state where $v \ne 0$.

sections.heading: 7. Trigonometric derivatives and applications
sections.body_md:
The quotient rule on $\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, $\dfrac{1}{\cos x}$, $\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$ and $\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ gives the derivatives of tangent, secant, cosecant and cotangent. The functions beginning with "co" carry a minus sign.

For a linear argument, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(ax + b) = a\cos(ax + b)$. Applications: the slope of the tangent at $x = a$ is $f'(a)$; the tangent is horizontal where $f'(x) = 0$; the rate of change of a quantity is its derivative.

key_terms.definition_md: The derivative of a quantity with respect to time (or another variable).
A tangent with slope $0$, found where $f'(x) = 0$.

rows: $\dfrac{\cos x \cdot \cos x - \sin x(-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} = \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x}$
$\dfrac{-\sin x \cdot \sin x - \cos x\cos x}{\sin^2 x} = -\dfrac{1}{\sin^2 x}$

visuals.caption: Product rule for one term, standard result for the other.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are usually awarded**
- *Rate of change or velocity (2-3 marks):* the quotient or derivative, then the value at the given time with units.
- *Tangent (2-3 marks):* the point, the slope from the derivative, then the equation.
- *First principles (2-3 marks):* the quotient written out, the simplified quotient with $h$ cancelled, then the limit.
- *Product or quotient (2-3 marks):* $u$, $v$, $u'$, $v'$, the rule written out, then the simplified result.
- *Trigonometric differentiation (2 marks):* each standard result, with its sign.
- *Long questions (5 marks, in parts):* the derivative first, then each later part (a value, a tangent, a rate) from it, with a check at one value.

**Common mistakes**
- Taking the limit before cancelling $h$, which gives $\dfrac{0}{0}$.
- Writing $(x + h)^2$ as $x^2 + h^2$.
- Using $u'v'$ for a product, or $uv' - u'v$ in the quotient rule.
- Missing the minus sign in the derivatives of cosine, cosecant and cotangent.
- Forgetting the factor $a$ when differentiating $\sin ax$.
- Using degrees instead of radians when differentiating a trigonometric function.

questions.stem_md: A hand-cart rolls along a straight track and its distance from the start after $t$ seconds is $s = t^2 + 5t$ metres. Its average velocity between $t = 1$ and $t = 3$ is
questions.solution_md: The average velocity is the change in distance divided by the time taken: $\dfrac{s(3) - s(1)}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{24 - 6}{2} = 9$ m/s. The value $18$ m/s is the change in distance $24 - 6$ left undivided; $11$ m/s is the instantaneous velocity $2t + 5$ at $t = 3$; $7$ m/s is the instantaneous velocity at $t = 1$.

questions.stem_md: For $f(x) = 3x^2$, the difference quotient $\dfrac{f(2 + h) - f(2)}{h}$ simplifies, for $h \ne 0$, to
questions.solution_md: $f(2 + h) - f(2) = 3(4 + 4h + h^2) - 12 = 12h + 3h^2$, and dividing by $h$ gives $12 + 3h$. The option $4 + h$ leaves out the factor $3$; $3h$ treats $(2 + h)^2$ as $4 + h^2$ and so loses the term $4h$; $12 + 3h^{2}$ divides only the first term by $h$.

questions.stem_md: A bead slides along a wire so that its distance from one end after $t$ seconds is $s = 2t^3 + t$ centimetres. Its velocity at $t = 2$ is
questions.solution_md: The velocity is $\dfrac{ds}{dt} = 6t^2 + 1$, which is $6(4) + 1 = 25$ cm/s at $t = 2$. The value $18$ cm/s is the distance $s(2) = 16 + 2$, not the velocity; $13$ cm/s uses $6t + 1$; $24$ cm/s forgets that $t$ has derivative $1$.

questions.stem_md: The curve $y = x^2 - 3x + 5$ passes through $(2, 3)$. The tangent to the curve at this point is the line
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2x - 3$, which is $1$ at $x = 2$. The tangent is $y - 3 = 1(x - 2)$, that is $y = x + 1$. The line $y = 4x - 5$ uses the slope $2x = 4$ and forgets $-3$; $y = x + 3$ keeps the slope but takes the constant as $f(2) = 3$; $y = -x + 5$ has the slope of the perpendicular.

questions.stem_md: In differentiating $x^4$ from the definition, the quotient $\dfrac{(x + h)^4 - x^4}{h}$ is simplified, for $h \ne 0$, to
questions.solution_md: $(x + h)^4 = x^4 + 4x^3h + 6x^2h^2 + 4xh^3 + h^4$, so the numerator is $4x^3h + 6x^2h^2 + 4xh^3 + h^4$ and dividing by $h$ gives $4x^3 + 6x^2h + 4xh^2 + h^3$. The option $4x^{3} + 6x^{2}h + 4xh^{2} + h^{4}$ leaves the last term as $h^4$; $4x^{3} + 4x^{2}h + 4xh^{2} + h^{3}$ uses the coefficients $4, 4, 4$ instead of $4, 6, 4$; $x^{3} + 3x^{2}h + 3xh^{2} + h^{3}$ is the quotient for $x^3$, not $x^4$.

questions.stem_md: Using the definition of the derivative, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{x + 5}\right)$, for $x \ne -5$, is found to be
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{h}\left[\dfrac{1}{x + h + 5} - \dfrac{1}{x + 5}\right] = \dfrac{1}{h} \cdot \dfrac{-h}{(x + h + 5)(x + 5)} = -\dfrac{1}{(x + h + 5)(x + 5)}$, which tends to $-\dfrac{1}{(x + 5)^2}$. The option $\dfrac{1}{(x + 5)^{2}}$ loses the sign from $(x + 5) - (x + h + 5) = -h$; $\dfrac{-1}{x + 5}$ forgets to square; $\dfrac{-1}{x^{2}}$ is the derivative of $\dfrac{1}{x}$, ignoring the shift by $5$.

questions.stem_md: From first principles, $\dfrac{\sin(3x + 3h) - \sin 3x}{h}$ equals $3\cos\left(3x + \dfrac{3h}{2}\right)\dfrac{\sin(3h/2)}{3h/2}$, so the derivative of $\sin 3x$ is
questions.solution_md: As $h \to 0$, $\cos\left(3x + \dfrac{3h}{2}\right) \to \cos 3x$ and $\dfrac{\sin(3h/2)}{3h/2} \to 1$, so the derivative is $3\cos 3x$. The option $\cos 3x$ forgets the factor $3$ that comes from the argument $3h$; $-3\cos 3x$ has the wrong sign; $3\sin 3x$ confuses sine and cosine.

questions.stem_md: The limit $\lim_{x \to 4}\dfrac{\sqrt{x} - 2}{x - 4}$ is the derivative of $\sqrt{x}$ at $x = 4$. Its value is
questions.solution_md: Multiplying by the conjugate, $\dfrac{\sqrt{x} - 2}{x - 4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x} + 2}$, which tends to $\dfrac{1}{4}$. The value $\dfrac{1}{8}$ comes from $\dfrac{1}{2x}$; $2$ is $\sqrt{4}$ itself; $\dfrac{1}{2}$ is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$.

questions.stem_md: The function $y = (x^2 + 1)(x^3 - 2x)$ is differentiated by the product rule. The result, written as a polynomial, is
questions.solution_md: With $u = x^2 + 1$ and $v = x^3 - 2x$: $u'v + uv' = 2x(x^3 - 2x) + (x^2 + 1)(3x^2 - 2) = 5x^4 - 3x^2 - 2$. The option $6x^{3} - 4x$ multiplies the two derivatives; $-x^{4} - 5x^{2} + 2$ subtracts, as the quotient rule does; $5x^{4} - 3x^{2} - 2x$ writes the derivative of $-2x$ as $-2x$.

questions.stem_md: For $x \ne 3$, differentiating $\dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}$ by the quotient rule gives
questions.solution_md: With $u = 2x + 1$, $v = x - 3$: $\dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2} = \dfrac{2(x - 3) - (2x + 1)}{(x - 3)^2} = \dfrac{-7}{(x - 3)^2}$. The option $\dfrac{7}{(x - 3)^{2}}$ subtracts in the wrong order; $2$ divides $u'$ by $v'$; $\dfrac{-7}{x - 3}$ does not square the denominator.

questions.stem_md: Differentiating $5\sin x - 2\cos x + 3x^2$ with respect to $x$ gives
questions.solution_md: Term by term: $5\cos x - 2(-\sin x) + 6x = 5\cos x + 2\sin x + 6x$. The option $5\cos x - 2\sin x + 6x$ forgets that $\cos x$ has derivative $-\sin x$; $-5\cos x + 2\sin x + 6x$ gives $\sin x$ the derivative $-\cos x$; $5\cos x + 2\sin x + 3x$ differentiates $3x^2$ as $3x$.

questions.stem_md: For $y = \tan x - \cot x$, at values of $x$ where both terms are defined, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan x) = \sec^2 x$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cot x) = -\operatorname{cosec}^2 x$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \sec^2 x + \operatorname{cosec}^2 x$. The option $\sec^{2} x - \operatorname{cosec}^{2} x$ loses the minus sign of the cotangent derivative; $\sec x\tan x + \operatorname{cosec} x\cot x$ uses the derivatives of secant and cosecant; $\cos^{2} x + \sin^{2} x$ inverts the two standard results.

questions.stem_md: For $0 < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, the derivative of $x\sec x$ is
questions.solution_md: By the product rule with $u = x$ and $v = \sec x$: $1 \cdot \sec x + x \sec x\tan x$. The option $\sec x\tan x$ differentiates only $\sec x$; $\sec x + x\sec^{2} x$ gives $\sec x$ the derivative $\sec^2 x$; $x\sec x\tan x$ omits the term $u'v$.

questions.stem_md: The function $y = \dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}$ is defined for $x \ne \pi, 3\pi, \dots$. Its derivative simplifies to
questions.solution_md: With $u = \sin x$, $v = 1 + \cos x$: the numerator is $\cos x(1 + \cos x) - \sin x(-\sin x) = \cos x + \cos^2 x + \sin^2 x = 1 + \cos x$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1 + \cos x}{(1 + \cos x)^2} = \dfrac{1}{1 + \cos x}$. The option $\dfrac{\cos x}{(1 + \cos x)^{2}}$ keeps only the term $u'v$; $\dfrac{\cos x + \cos 2x}{(1 + \cos x)^{2}}$ adds $uv'$ instead of subtracting it; $-\cot x$ divides $u'$ by $v'$.

questions.stem_md: The tangent to the curve $y = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x - 4$ is parallel to the $x$-axis at the points whose $x$-coordinates are
questions.solution_md: The slope is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6x^2 - 18x + 12 = 6(x - 1)(x - 2)$, which is zero at $x = 1$ and $x = 2$. The pair $-1, -2$ changes the signs of the roots; $0, 3$ are the roots of $x^2 - 3x$ with the constant $12$ forgotten; $1, 3$ come from reading $-18x \div 6$ as $-4x$.

questions.stem_md: If $f(x) = x\cos x$, then $f'\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ equals
questions.solution_md: $f'(x) = \cos x - x\sin x$, so $f'\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0 - \dfrac{\pi}{2}(1) = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. The value $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ uses $\cos x + x\sin x$; $-1$ multiplies the two derivatives, $1 \cdot (-\sin x)$; $0$ keeps only the term $u'v = \cos x$.

questions.stem_md: A water tank holds $V = 300 + 40t - t^2$ litres, $t$ minutes after a valve is opened. At $t = 5$ the volume is changing at the rate of
questions.solution_md: The rate of change is $\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 40 - 2t$, which is $40 - 10 = 30$ litres per minute at $t = 5$. The value $35$ uses $40 - t$; $40$ ignores the term $-t^2$; $95$ divides the volume $V(5) = 475$ by the time, $\dfrac{475}{5}$.

questions.stem_md: A body moves along a line with distance $s(t)$ from a fixed point. Its instantaneous velocity at the time $t = a$ is defined as

options.text_md: $\dfrac{s(a + 1) - s(a)}{1}$, the change over one second

questions.solution_md: The instantaneous velocity is the limit of the average velocities over $[a, a + h]$ as $h \to 0$, that is $\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{s(a + h) - s(a)}{h}$. The quotient over one second is only the average velocity over a whole second; the expression with $s(a + h) + s(a)$ adds instead of subtracting, so it does not even settle; and $\lim_{h \to 0}\left[s(a + h) - s(a)\right]$ has no division by $h$ and always tends to $0$.

questions.stem_md: A student differentiates $f(x) = x^2$ from the definition by writing $\dfrac{(x + h)^2 - x^2}{h} = \dfrac{x^2 + h^2 - x^2}{h} = h$, and concludes that $f'(x) = 0$. The mistake in this working is that

options.text_md: the quotient should have been divided by $x$ and not by $h$
$f'(x)$ should be found by putting $h = 1$ before simplifying
$(x + h)^2$ was written as $x^2 + h^2$, leaving out the term $2xh$
the limit should have been taken as $h \to \infty$

questions.solution_md: $(x + h)^2 = x^2 + 2xh + h^2$, not $x^2 + h^2$. The correct quotient is $\dfrac{2xh + h^2}{h} = 2x + h$, which tends to $2x$. Taking $h \to \infty$, dividing by $x$ or putting $h = 1$ is not what the definition says.

questions.stem_md: Let $u = x^2$ and $v = x^3$. The derivative of the product $uv$ equals the product $u'v'$ of the two derivatives exactly when
questions.solution_md: $(uv)' = (x^5)' = 5x^4$ and $u'v' = 2x \cdot 3x^2 = 6x^3$. Equating, $5x^4 - 6x^3 = x^3(5x - 6) = 0$, so $x = 0$ or $x = \dfrac{6}{5}$. The product of derivatives is therefore not the derivative of the product in general.

questions.stem_md: True or false: for a distance-time function $s(t)$, the derivative $s'(a)$ is the instantaneous velocity of the moving body at the time $t = a$.
questions.solution_md: True. The derivative $s'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{s(a + h) - s(a)}{h}$ is the limit of the average velocities, which is the velocity at that instant. For $s = t^2$ at $t = 3$ it is $6$.

questions.stem_md: True or false: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^3 \cdot x^4\right) = 3x^2 \cdot 4x^3$.
questions.solution_md: False. The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives. Here $x^3 \cdot x^4 = x^7$ has derivative $7x^6$, while $3x^2 \cdot 4x^3 = 12x^5$.

questions.stem_md: True or false: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{cosec} x) = \operatorname{cosec} x\cot x$ wherever $\sin x \ne 0$.
questions.solution_md: False. The correct result is $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{cosec} x) = -\operatorname{cosec} x\cot x$, with a minus sign, as for every function whose name begins with "co".

questions.stem_md: True or false: from first principles, the derivative of $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ at $x = 2$ is $-\dfrac{1}{4}$.
questions.solution_md: True. $\dfrac{f(2 + h) - f(2)}{h} = -\dfrac{1}{2(2 + h)}$, which tends to $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ as $h \to 0$.

questions.stem_md: True or false: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[(3x + 2)^2\right] = 18x + 12$.
questions.solution_md: True. Expanding first, $(3x + 2)^2 = 9x^2 + 12x + 4$, whose derivative is $18x + 12$.

questions.stem_md: A trolley's distance from the start after $t$ seconds is $s = t^2$ metres. Its instantaneous velocity at $t = 4$ s is ___ m/s.
questions.solution_md: The velocity is $\dfrac{ds}{dt} = 2t$, which is $2(4) = 8$ m/s at $t = 4$.

questions.stem_md: For $u = x^2$ and $v = x + 1$, the derivative of the product $uv$ at $x = 1$ is ___.
questions.solution_md: By the product rule $(uv)' = u'v + uv' = 2x(x + 1) + x^2(1)$, which is $4 + 1 = 5$ at $x = 1$.

questions.solution_md: At $x = 2$ the quotient is $12 + 6h + h^2$, which tends to $12$ as $h \to 0$.

questions.stem_md: The slope of the curve $y = \cos x$ at the point where $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ is ___ (give an exact fraction).
questions.solution_md: The slope is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\sin x$, which is $-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, that is -1/2.

questions.stem_md: A sled slides so that its distance from the top of a slope is $s = 2t^2 + t$ metres after $t$ seconds. Find its average velocity (in m/s) from $t = 1$ to $t = 4$.
questions.solution_md: $s(4) = 36$ and $s(1) = 3$, so the average velocity is $\dfrac{36 - 3}{4 - 1} = \dfrac{33}{3} = 11$ m/s.

questions.stem_md: The graph of $y = x^4 - 3x^2$ has a tangent at the point with $x = 2$. Find the gradient of this tangent.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4x^3 - 6x$, so the gradient at $x = 2$ is $4(8) - 6(2) = 32 - 12 = 20$.

For $f(x) = 3\sin x - 4\cos x + x$, find $f'\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$, correct to two decimal places.
questions.solution_md: $f'(x) = 3\cos x + 4\sin x + 1$, so $f'\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} + 4 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 1 = 2.5 + 2\sqrt{3} = 5.96$ to two decimal places.

questions.stem_md: The tangent to the curve $y = x^2 + 2x + 3$ at the point where $x = -2$ meets the $y$-axis at the point $(0, k)$. Find $k$.
questions.solution_md: At $x = -2$: $y = 4 - 4 + 3 = 3$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2x + 2 = -2$. The tangent is $y - 3 = -2(x + 2)$, so $y = -2x - 1$ and $k = -1$.

questions.stem_md: A culture contains $N = 500 + 60t - 4t^2$ thousand cells $t$ hours after it is set up. At what time $t$ (in hours) is the count changing at $12$ thousand cells per hour?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = 60 - 8t$. Setting $60 - 8t = 12$ gives $8t = 48$, so $t = 6$ hours.

questions.stem_md: A toboggan runs so that its distance from the start is $s = 4t^2 + t$ metres after $t$ seconds. Find its average velocity on the interval from $t = 2$ to $t = 2 + h$, and deduce its velocity at $t = 2$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$s(2 + h) - s(2) = 4(2 + h)^2 + (2 + h) - 18 = 16 + 16h + 4h^2 + 2 + h - 18 = 17h + 4h^2$.
Average velocity $= \dfrac{17h + 4h^2}{h} = 17 + 4h$ m/s.
As $h \to 0$ this tends to $17$, so the velocity at $t = 2$ is $17$ m/s.

The tangent is $y - 4 = 5(x - 2)$, that is $y = 5x - 6$.

questions.stem_md: A rail wagon is at the distance $s = t^3 + 2t$ metres from the depot after $t$ seconds. Find its average velocity from $t = 1$ to $t = 2$, and find its velocity at $t = 1$ as a limit.

answer.model_answer_md:

$s(1 + h) - s(1) = (1 + 3h + 3h^2 + h^3) + 2 + 2h - 3 = 5h + 3h^2 + h^3$, so the quotient is $5 + 3h + h^2$.
As $h \to 0$ this tends to $5$, so the velocity at $t = 1$ is $5$ m/s.

questions.stem_md: Differentiate $\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ with respect to $x$ from first principles, for $x \ne 0$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{1}{h}\left[\dfrac{1}{(x + h)^2} - \dfrac{1}{x^2}\right] = \dfrac{x^2 - (x + h)^2}{h\,x^2(x + h)^2} = \dfrac{-2xh - h^2}{h\,x^2(x + h)^2} = -\dfrac{2x + h}{x^2(x + h)^2}$.
As $h \to 0$ this tends to $-\dfrac{2x}{x^4}$.
So $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) = -\dfrac{2}{x^3}$.

questions.stem_md: Find the derivative of $\sqrt{x + 4}$ for $x > -4$ using the definition.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{\sqrt{x + h + 4} - \sqrt{x + 4}}{h} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{x + h + 4} + \sqrt{x + 4}}{\sqrt{x + h + 4} + \sqrt{x + 4}} = \dfrac{(x + h + 4) - (x + 4)}{h\left(\sqrt{x + h + 4} + \sqrt{x + 4}\right)}$.
Cancelling $h$ gives $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x + h + 4} + \sqrt{x + 4}}$.
As $h \to 0$ the derivative is $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x + 4}}$.

questions.stem_md: Prove from first principles that $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos 3x) = -3\sin 3x$, using $\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\sin h}{h} = 1$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\cos(3x + 3h) - \cos 3x = -2\sin\left(3x + \dfrac{3h}{2}\right)\sin\dfrac{3h}{2}$.
So the quotient is $-3\sin\left(3x + \dfrac{3h}{2}\right)\cdot\dfrac{\sin(3h/2)}{3h/2}$.
As $h \to 0$, $\sin\left(3x + \dfrac{3h}{2}\right) \to \sin 3x$ and $\dfrac{\sin(3h/2)}{3h/2} \to 1$, so the derivative is $-3\sin 3x$.

questions.stem_md: Obtain the derivative of $x^2\sin x - 2x\cos x$, writing it as one expression in $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2\sin x) = 2x\sin x + x^2\cos x$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}(2x\cos x) = 2\cos x - 2x\sin x$.
Subtracting: $2x\sin x + x^2\cos x - 2\cos x + 2x\sin x$.
Collecting, the derivative is $4x\sin x + (x^2 - 2)\cos x$.

With $u = x^2 + 3$ and $v = \cot x$: $u' = 2x$ and $v' = -\operatorname{cosec}^2 x$.
$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[(x^2 + 3)\cot x\right] = 2x\cot x + (x^2 + 3)\left(-\operatorname{cosec}^2 x\right) = 2x\cot x - (x^2 + 3)\operatorname{cosec}^2 x$.

questions.stem_md: The graph of $y = x - 2\sin x$ has a tangent at its point with abscissa $\pi$. Write the equation of that tangent.

A robot arm moves its tip along a rail so that its distance from the home position is $s = 2t^2 + 3t$ centimetres after $t$ seconds.

(a) Find the average velocity of the tip from $t = 2$ to $t = 4$. [1]

(b) Find its velocity at $t = 2$ by taking the limit of the difference quotient. [2]

(c) Write the equation of the tangent to the $s$-$t$ graph at $t = 2$. [1]

(d) At what time is the velocity equal to the average velocity found in (a)? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $s(2) = 14$ and $s(4) = 44$, so the average velocity is $\dfrac{44 - 14}{2} = 15$ cm/s.

(b) $s(2 + h) - s(2) = 2(4 + 4h + h^2) + 6 + 3h - 14 = 11h + 2h^2$, so the quotient is $11 + 2h$. As $h \to 0$ the velocity at $t = 2$ is $11$ cm/s.

(c) The slope is $11$ and the point is $(2, 14)$: $s - 14 = 11(t - 2)$, that is $s = 11t - 8$.

(d) The velocity is $\dfrac{ds}{dt} = 4t + 3$. Setting $4t + 3 = 15$ gives $t = 3$ seconds.

questions.solution_md: Average velocity over an interval, then the limit of the quotient from $t = 2$, the tangent, and the equation $4t + 3 = 15$.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Prove from first principles that $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \cos x$, using $\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\sin h}{h} = 1$ and $\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h} = 0$. [3]

(b) Hence find all values of $x$ in $[0, 2\pi]$ at which the tangent to $y = \sin x$ has slope $\dfrac{1}{2}$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\sin(x + h) = \sin x\cos h + \cos x\sin h$, so $\dfrac{\sin(x + h) - \sin x}{h} = \sin x \cdot \dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h} + \cos x \cdot \dfrac{\sin h}{h}$.
As $h \to 0$ the two limits are $0$ and $1$, so $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \sin x(0) + \cos x(1) = \cos x$.

(b) The slope is $\cos x$. Setting $\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ in $[0, 2\pi]$ gives $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $x = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$.

questions.solution_md: Split the quotient into a sine part and a cosine part; the slope is the derivative.

questions.stem_md:
Let $y = x\cos x - \sin x$ and $z = \dfrac{\sin x}{x^2 + 1}$.

(a) Show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -x\sin x$. [2]

(b) Find $\dfrac{dz}{dx}$. [2]

(c) Find the value of $\dfrac{dz}{dx}$ at $x = 0$. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) By the product rule $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x) = \cos x - x\sin x$, and $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \cos x$. So $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \cos x - x\sin x - \cos x = -x\sin x$.

(b) With $u = \sin x$ and $v = x^2 + 1$: $\dfrac{dz}{dx} = \dfrac{\cos x(x^2 + 1) - \sin x(2x)}{(x^2 + 1)^2}$.

(c) At $x = 0$: $\dfrac{1(1) - 0}{1} = 1$.

questions.solution_md: The terms in $\cos x$ cancel in part (a); in (b) name $u'$ and $v'$ first.

questions.stem_md:
The curve $C$ is $y = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 2$.

(a) Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$. [1]

(b) Find the points of $C$ at which the tangent is parallel to the $x$-axis. [2]

(c) Find the equation of the tangent to $C$ at the point where $x = 2$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 - 12x + 9$.

(b) Setting $3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x - 1)(x - 3) = 0$ gives $x = 1$ and $x = 3$. Then $y = 1 - 6 + 9 + 2 = 6$ and $y = 27 - 54 + 27 + 2 = 2$, so the points are $(1, 6)$ and $(3, 2)$.

(c) At $x = 2$: $y = 8 - 24 + 18 + 2 = 4$ and the slope is $12 - 24 + 9 = -3$. The tangent is $y - 4 = -3(x - 2)$, that is $y = -3x + 10$.

questions.solution_md: A tangent parallel to the $x$-axis has slope $0$.

questions.stem_md:
The horizontal displacement of a pendulum bob from its rest position is $x = 4\sin 3t$ centimetres, $t$ seconds after release.

(a) Find the velocity $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ in terms of $t$. [2]

(b) Find the velocity at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{9}$. [1]

(c) Find the first time $t > 0$ at which the bob is momentarily at rest, and its displacement then. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For a linear argument, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(\sin 3t) = 3\cos 3t$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 4 \cdot 3\cos 3t = 12\cos 3t$ cm/s.

(b) At $t = \dfrac{\pi}{9}$: $12\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 12 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 6$ cm/s.

(c) At rest means $12\cos 3t = 0$. The first positive solution has $3t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ seconds. Then $x = 4\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 4$ cm.

questions.solution_md: At rest means zero velocity, so solve $\cos 3t = 0$.
